description_ru: Как грибы соединяют корни деревьев в подземную сеть, что показали опыты Сюзанны Симард и почему учёные до сих пор спорят о её роли.
text:
Beneath the soil of any forest lies a landscape more crowded than the one above it. Threads of fungi, many of them finer than a human hair, thread through the dirt in their millions of kilometres, and a great number of them are attached to the roots of trees. The arrangement is called a mycorrhiza, from the Greek for fungus and root, and it is among the oldest and most successful partnerships on Earth. Roughly nine out of every ten species of land plant form some version of it.

The bargain is an elegant one. A tree captures sunlight and builds sugars, which it cannot eat all at once. A fungus has no leaves at all but excels at foraging, reaching with its slender filaments into places no root can enter, and extracting phosphorus, nitrogen, and water. The tree pays the fungus in sugar; the fungus pays the tree in minerals. Neither is acting out of kindness. Each is a pragmatist who has discovered that cooperation, on balance, beats isolation.

The idea that this partnership might also connect the trees to one another gained fame in 1997, when a Canadian ecologist named Suzanne Simard published a study in the journal Nature. Working in British Columbia, her team planted seedlings of paper birch and Douglas fir, then labelled the carbon in some of them with a radioactive tracer. Within days, traces of the tracer turned up in neighbouring seedlings of the other species. Carbon, it seemed, had travelled between trees, presumably through a shared fungal network. Journalists, never ones to waste a good phrase, christened it the wood wide web.

The story that grew from it was irresistible. Older "mother trees" were said to nurture their young, to warn neighbours of insect attacks, and even to send sugar to the shaded seedlings that struggled beneath them. Documentaries wept over the generosity of the forest.

Science, fortunately, is not sentimental. In recent years, several researchers have examined the evidence with a cooler eye. A review published in 2023 by Justine Karst and her colleagues found that some of the most popular claims rested on surprisingly thin foundations. Few studies, they argued, had shown that the carbon transferred through the fungi actually improved a seedling's survival in a natural forest, and the notion of mother trees consciously feeding their offspring had been repeated far more often than it had been tested. Simard and others have replied that the field is difficult, that fungal networks are hard to observe without destroying them, and that the effect is real even if its scale is debated.

It is possible both camps are partly right. Nobody seriously doubts that fungi link plants, or that nutrients move through the links. The open questions are how much moves, in which directions, and with what consequences for the trees. A fungus is not a charitable water pipe. It is an organism with its own appetites, and it may well be steering the flow to its own advantage.

For the curious visitor, this is the pleasure of the subject. The forest is neither the tender community of the documentaries nor the cold marketplace of the sceptics, but something stranger: a negotiation, conducted in the dark, in a language of chemistry that we are only beginning to read.

questions.answer: A partnership between a fungus and plant roots.
